newsitem.title: USA: Plaintiffs hail Simpson damages; advocates cry foul.
newsitem.headline: Plaintiffs hail Simpson damages; advocates cry foul.

text.p: The staggering $25 million civil award of punitive damages against O.J. Simpson for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend was hailed by plaintiffs' lawyers on Monday, but Simpson advocates cried foul.
"This verdict is illegal. I guarantee there's going to be an appeal," Leo Terrell, an attorney and sometime Simpson family spokesman said outside the courthouse.
"This is wrong. This is against the law. You can't award more money than the man has under punitive damages," an angry Terrell told local KCAL television.

He branded the $25 million award from the former football star, actor and television pitchman excessive, saying it was way outside California court guidelines based on 30 percent of a defendant's worth, including potential future earnings.
Attorney Johnnie Cochran, who led Simpson's successful criminal trial defence, also questioned the amount the jury ordered the ex-football star to pay.
The $25 million in punitive damages, on top of $8.5 million already awarded in compensatory damages, "probably violated state law..." he said.

"You're not supposed to leave anyone penniless," Cochran told ABC radio. "Even under the best case scenario, the plaintiffs said he (Simpson) had $15 million and they (the jury) awarded them $25 million, so they gave them more than the plaintiffs said he had, even in the future."
When asked how the Simpson family reacted, Terrell said "They are upset because this verdict is illegal. That's the best I can say and that's the consensus among family members."

None of Simpson's civil trial legal team made any comment and left the Santa Monica courthouse after winning a 10-day stay in the damages award during which time they are expected to file an appeal or a motion to reduce the award.

Victorious plaintiffs' lawyer Daniel Petrocelli acknowledged it might be difficult to collect, but said the money was less important than having Simpson held publicly responsible for the deaths of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.

"It is not a concern; it is not our focus on how to collect," Petrocelli told reporters after the jury's verdict awarding $12.5 million for each of the deaths. "There is no reason to believe the award will be reduced at all."

"It was absolutely essential to call O.J. Simpson a killer and to treat O.J. Simpson as a killer," to sway the jury, said Petrocelli, finally freed of the gag-order on lawyers imposed by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki.
"We could not expect the jury to stand up to him (Simpson), if we didn't."
Michael Brewer, the attorney for Goldman's estranged mother, Sharon Rufo, praised the verdict too. "They collectively came to what we feel is the right verdict," he told KCAL.
Rufo, he said, was pleased because the jury "recognized someone was responsible for her son's death, that his life means something."
Attorney Gloria Allred, who has often represented the Brown family, spoke out for the children of Simpson and his slain ex-wife.

"This was a reprehensible, despicable and unconscionable act and they (the jury) sent that message through the $12.5 million damages they awarded the estate of Nicole Brown Simpson. The only heirs of that estate are Sydney and Justin and they are entitled to be compensated.
"Nothing can bring back their mother, but I think it is important that the jury has spoken to protect the children's future," she said on KCAL.
She said she expected the award to be "very, very high," since it is meant to punish, but it would be a "long road" to collect.

Asked about the effect the jury award would have on the custody battle, in which the Browns are attempting to overturn a judge's ruling giving Simpson custody of the children, Allred said: "There is more to come," adding an announcement might be made on Tuesday concerning the custody battle.
